title: The Full Moon
summary: A full moon rises and the king of mind is without stain; the guru's word cuts the stain of delusion, a seed like the sky spreads sky-wide and the shade of its own tree covers the three worlds; as sunrise clears the night and the swan king separates the waters, one eats existence, says Kāṇha. In his commentary, which also survives only in Tibetan, Munidatta reads the moon as the moon-disc of bodhicitta rising by the guru's kindness (cp.24.m2), and the last couplet as telling the yogin to eat existence without taking it up (cp.24.m6).

lines.translit: /dpa' bo'i ti la zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyi'o/
lines.gloss: hero's · ti la · called · melody · black (Kṛṣṇa) · of conduct · feet (honorific) · of (it is)

flags.note: The rāga name dpa' bo'i ti la is unidentified, so I keep it in Wylie. dpa' bo is the regular Tibetan for vīra, 'hero', while ti la looks like a transcription (of tila, 'sesame', or tilaka, 'forehead mark'?). The Tibetan may be half translating and half transcribing an Indian name, as it translates other rāga names (skya rengs for Aru, 'dod pa sbyin pa for Kāmoda). I have not guessed a Sanskrit form. I proposed a keep-source entry, dpa-boi-ti-la, so the heading links like the other rāga names.

The Tibetan names the poet nag po spyod pa'i zhabs, its usual translated form of Kṛṣṇācārya(pāda) (nag po, 'black', for Kṛṣṇa; spyod pa, 'conduct'; zhabs for the honorific -pāda). I render it with the glossary's Kāṇha plus -pāda, on the pattern 'Lūyīpāda'. In 5b the poet's name is transcribed instead (kAh+Na pa).

lines.translit: /gang tshe zla ba gang ba shar gyur pa/
lines.gloss: when · moon · full · risen · has become

lines.translit: /de tshe sems kyi rgyal po dri ma med/
lines.gloss: then · of mind · king · stain · is without
lines.en: then the [king of mind]{king-of-mind} is without [stain]{mala}.

flags.note: sems kyi rgyal po can also be read as apposition, 'the king that is the mind' (the mind as king). I keep the glossary's 'king of mind'. dri ma med, 'stain-less', is rendered 'without stain' so that the glossary's 'stain' can stand as it is.

lines.translit: /gti mug dri ma gcod pa bla ma'i gsungs/

flags.note: bla ma'i gsungs: a genitive followed by gsungs, which is normally the past of the honorific verb 'speak'. I read it as the noun gsung, 'the guru's word'. Munidatta's paraphrase, bla ma'i gsung gis, 'by the guru's word' (cp.24.m3), supports this reading. Another possible reading is 'the guru spoke of cutting the stain of delusion'.

gti mug dri ma: read as 'the stain of delusion' (compare Sanskrit mohamala). It could also be read as 'delusion and stain(s)'. Munidatta's paraphrase, 'the obscurations of delusion and the rest' (cp.24.m3), does not settle the question.

lines.translit: /yul dang dbang po nam mkhar sleb par 'gyur/
lines.gloss: objects · and · sense faculties · into the sky · to arrive · become (will)

flags.note: sleb par 'gyur, 'come to arrive', can be future ('will reach') or a general present. I give the present so that it matches 1b.

lines.translit: /mkha' mtshungs sa bon gang zhig mkha' mnyam 'gro/
lines.gloss: sky · like · seed · which · sky · equal · goes
lines.en: A [seed]{seed} like the [sky]{gagana}, which spreads as wide as the [sky]{gagana}:

flags.note: mkha' mnyam 'gro literally means 'goes sky-equal'. I use 'spreads', a sense 'gro has when fame 'goes' in all directions, together with 'as wide as the sky'. Other possible renderings: 'becomes equal to the sky' ('gro, 'become'), or 'goes as far as the sky'. mkha' mnyam 'gro (ba) is also the stock phrase 'beings as numberless as the sky', but that reading seems unlikely here. Munidatta does not gloss these words (cp.24.m4).
gang zhig can be a relative ('a seed ... which') or an indefinite ('whatever seed is like the sky spreads as wide as the sky'). I take 3a as the topic of which 3b speaks.

lines.translit: /rang gi shing las khams gsum grib mas khyab/
lines.gloss: own · tree · from · three worlds · by shade · pervaded
lines.en: shade from its own [tree]{tree} covers the [three worlds]{trailokya}.

flags.note: rang gi shing: I read it as 'its own tree', meaning the seed's tree, since the seed is the topic. It could also mean 'one's own tree', which is what the glossary's shade entry has. khyab, 'pervade', is rendered 'covers' because the subject is shade.

lines.translit: /ji ltar nyin byed shar bas mtshan mo sel bar byed/
lines.gloss: just as · day-maker (sun) · by rising · night · clearing · does
lines.en: Just as the rising [sun]{surya} clears away the [night]{night},

flags.note: This line has eleven syllables, where the rest of the song has nine. Perhaps sel bar byed was filled out from 4b; Munidatta's lemma is only mtshan mo sel (cp.24.m5). I translate the line as it stands.

lines.translit: /srid mtshor gti mug rab rib sel bar byed/
lines.gloss: in the ocean of existence · delusion · dim sight · clearing · does
lines.en: so it clears away the [dim sight]{dim-sight} of [delusion]{moha} in the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava}.

flags.note: The Tibetan has no subject here and no correlative (de bzhin) answering the ji ltar of 4a, so I supply 'so it'. The subject may be the sun of 4a, continuing the simile, or something the song named earlier (the guru's word, the stainless king of mind). Munidatta links the clearing to bowing to the true guru's feet (cp.24.m5). Another option is to leave the subject unexpressed with a passive: 'so the dim sight of delusion is cleared away'.

lines.translit: /ji ltar dang pa'i rgyal pos chu bo 'byed/
lines.gloss: just as · of the clear (read ngang pa'i, of the swan) · by the king · river, water · separates
lines.en: Just as the [swan king]{swan-king} separates the waters,

flags.note: The Tibetan reads dang pa'i rgyal pos. Taken literally this is 'the king of the clear' (dang ba, 'clear, limpid'), and 'the first king' would need a further change to dang po'i. Neither makes sense with 'separates the waters'. Munidatta's lemma reads ngang pa'i rgyal po, 'swan king', and explains it by the swan's separating water from milk (cp.24.m6). The two readings differ by one letter (ང for ད). I emend and translate 'swan king'; translit keeps the witness's dang pa'i.

chu bo usually means 'river', but here it is what the swan king separates: in Munidatta's comment, water mixed with milk (cp.24.m6). 'The waters' leaves room for both senses; 'the river' would keep the dictionary sense. A bare guess: chu bo might be a slip for chu 'o, 'water and milk'.

lines.translit: /srid pa za zhes kAh+Na pa yis smra/
lines.gloss: existence · eats · thus (quote) · Kāṇha · by · says

flags.note: srid pa za zhes: za is the present stem, 'eats' (the imperative would be zo), and no subject is given. I render 'one eats' and supply 'so' to complete the ji ltar of 5a. Munidatta takes the line as an injunction: existence is to be eaten, and 'you must not take up existence' (cp.24.m6). On that reading the line would be 'eat existence, says Kāṇha'.
Here the poet's name is transcribed, kAh+Na pa (the vernacular Kāhna/Kāṇha with the Tibetan suffix -pa). The heading uses the translated form nag po spyod pa'i zhabs instead. Both are rendered Kāṇha.

notes.text: The original of this song is lost. The Nepal palm-leaf manuscript edited by Shastri lacks song 24, and no Old Bengali text survives. This is a translation of the Tibetan translation, the song as quoted in the Tibetan version of the commentary (Degé Tengyur, Toh 2293, made by Kīrticandra and Drakpa Gyaltsen in Yambu). No Bengali original is reconstructed here, and the transliteration gives the Tibetan in Wylie.

Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each heading names the rāga the song is sung to; here the Tibetan word is glu dbyangs, 'melody'. The name itself, dpa' bo'i ti la, is kept in Wylie because the Indian name behind it has not been identified. dpa' bo is the regular Tibetan for vīra, 'hero', while ti la looks transcribed. The name may therefore be half translated and half transcribed, as the Tibetan handles other rāga names (skya rengs, 'dawn', for Aru; lha rnams rol pa for Devakrī).

Munidatta opens by saying that Kṛṣṇācārya (nag po spyod pa pa) meditates once again on that same meaning, the king of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, through the taste of the [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of all things (cp.24.m1).

Munidatta reads the full moon as the moon-disc (zla ba'i dkyil 'khor) of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, 'the mind of awakening', complete with its [sixteen digits]{sixteen-digits}, which rises by the guru's kindness. At that time, he says, the lord of yogis, the king of mind, becomes utterly stainless (cp.24.m2). The song itself names neither the guru nor bodhicitta in this couplet.

In Indian reckoning the moon has sixteen digits (kalā), the portions by which it waxes, and all of them are present at the full moon. The song opens on that image of completeness, and on the mind pictured as a king.

Munidatta says the refrain makes that same meaning firm. For one with understanding, he says, the obscurations of delusion and the rest flee by the guru's word; the song's verb is 'cut'. Sense objects and senses 'enter the sky, the [clear light]{prabhasvara}'. He then cites [Saraha]{p-saraha}: 'homage to that which has dawned all at once' (cp.24.m3).

Literally, a seed like the sky spreads as wide as the sky, and shade from 'its own tree' (rang gi shing) covers the three worlds. It is as if the seed had grown into a tree that shades the whole world. In Buddhist cosmology the three worlds (khams gsum) are the realms of desire, form and formlessness.

Munidatta calls this couplet his second verse and says it teaches the power of the seed of dharma. The seed like the sky is born from the mind whose nature is [clear light]{prabhasvara}, and its nature, utterly luminous, is the shade of one's own tree. The shade pervading the three worlds is the lord of yogis pervading them with the rays of [knowledge]{jnana} (cp.24.m4). His gloss has 'jig rten gsum po where the song has khams gsum.
nyin byed, 'day-maker', is a poetic word for the sun (compare Sanskrit divākara). Munidatta's paraphrase has nyin mor byed pa, which means the same (cp.24.m5).

rab rib, 'dim sight', regularly renders Sanskrit timira. This is an eye disorder that makes one see hairs, specks or a double moon that are not there, and it is a stock Buddhist image of false appearance. Here delusion is that film over the eyes, cleared as sunrise clears the night. The ocean of existence (srid mtsho) is the round of rebirth pictured as a sea.

Munidatta calls this couplet his third verse and says it states its particular characteristic. As the rising sun clears the darkness of night, so for one who bows deeply to the dust of the true guru's feet, by the kindness of what is born of discernment, the obscurations of delusion, hatred and the rest go far off in the ocean of existence (cp.24.m5). He does not single out 'dim sight'.

The Tibetan line reads dang pa'i rgyal pos. With dang ba, 'clear, limpid', this could only mean 'the king of the clear', and 'the first king' would need a further change to dang po'i. Neither reading suits a king who separates the waters. Munidatta's lemma reads ngang pa'i rgyal po, 'swan king', and he explains it at once: outwardly the swan king separates water mixed with milk and drinks the milk (cp.24.m6). The difference is a single letter (ང nga for ད da). The draft emends to ngang pa'i and translates 'swan king'; the transliteration keeps what the witness has.

Indian poetry credits the haṃsa (Tibetan ngang pa, a goose or swan) with separating milk from water and drinking only the milk, a stock figure for discernment. The line's chu bo usually means 'river'. 'The waters' leaves the line open between a river and the water the bird separates.

Munidatta calls this couplet his fourth verse, on the conduct of the lord of yogis. After the outward example of the swan king he turns to Kāṇha himself ('O supreme yogin'): understanding the nature of existence through reality itself, existence is to be eaten, and 'you must not take up existence'. He supports this with a verse from the [Jñānasaṃbodhi]{tx-jnanasambodhi}: 'neither existence nor [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, from realizing the real as it is' (cp.24.m6). He therefore takes the song's 'eats' as an injunction.

termsOmitted.reason: Here chu bo names the water the swan king separates, which Munidatta describes as water mixed with milk (cp.24.m6), rather than a river as a place. I render it 'the waters' and flag the choice; the reviewer may prefer 'the river'.

proposals.definition: The name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 24 is sung, known only from the Tibetan heading. dpa' bo is the regular Tibetan for vīra, 'hero'; ti la looks like a transcription, perhaps of tila or tilaka. The Indian name behind it is not identified, so the Wylie is kept.
proposals.rationale: Every other rāga name in the headings has an entry (aru, bhairavi, devakri, gauda and others). This entry lets the heading link the same way and gives the reviewer one place to record an identification if one is found. It is provisional: the name is unidentified and occurs only here.

questions: 5a: I emend dang pa'i to ngang pa'i, 'swan king', on the strength of Munidatta's lemma and gloss (cp.24.m6), and keep dang pa'i in translit. Do you accept the emendation, and should translit print the emended form or mark it?
5a: I render chu bo, usually 'river', as 'the waters' and list the river entry in termsOmitted. Would you rather keep the image as 'the river'?

5b: za is a plain present ('eats'), so I give 'so one eats existence'. Munidatta reads an injunction (existence is to be eaten; do not take it up, cp.24.m6). Should the line be 'eat existence, says Kāṇha'?
3a: I render mkha' mnyam 'gro as 'spreads as wide as the sky'. The alternatives are 'becomes equal to the sky' and 'goes as far as the sky'. Which do you prefer?
4b and 5b: the Tibetan has ji ltar, 'just as', with no answering de bzhin and no subject. I supply 'so it' and 'so one'. Is that acceptable, or should the subject stay unexpressed?
Heading: I keep the rāga name dpa' bo'i ti la in Wylie and propose a keep-source entry to match the other rāga names. Can you identify the Indian name, and do you want the entry at all?
Heading: the Tibetan names the poet nag po spyod pa'i zhabs (Kṛṣṇācārya), and I write Kāṇhapāda using the glossary's Kāṇha. Keep that, or follow the Tibetan's Kṛṣṇācārya?
